Medicaid "savings" often mean bureaucratic shell games—real reform requires slashing waste, not shifting funds. The American Land and Property Protection Act? Long overdue. Federal overreach has strangled property rights for decades, with agencies like the EPA and Interior Department weaponizing regulations to seize control.

Sarah Lynn Migrim’s tragic death highlights the urgent need to crush antisemitic violence—weak leadership enabled this rot. Small businesses and veterans drive America’s economy, yet D.C. prioritizes foreign aid over domestic strength.

Until Congress guts bloated programs and redirects every dollar to secure borders, energy dominance, and law enforcement, these “recaps” are just more political theater.

Medicaid’s real problem? Bloated bureaucracy and Big Pharma’s grip on pricing—not the beneficiaries. The One Big Beautiful Bill’s work requirements miss the mark. Section 3(b) funnels $200B into pharmaceutical middlemen while Section 5(d) preserves loopholes for insurance consultants.

If Congress wants to “preserve” Medicaid, start by slashing overpayments to drug companies and ending redundant billing schemes. Redirect those savings to block grants for states—actual reform, not performative hurdles.

Until then, this bill’s just another handout to lobbyists disguised as fiscal responsibility.

Rural hospitals are collapsing under decades of bureaucratic bloat and Medicaid fraud—throwing $50B at the problem without structural reform is just another DC band-aid. The One Big Beautiful Bill’s rural health fund (H.R.1) was a rushed political trade-off to pass broader cuts, not a real solution.

Missouri’s Homer G. Phillips closure proves temporary cash infusions can’t fix systemic rot: payroll implosions, vendor lawsuits, and regulatory failure. This $50B will likely flow to admin consultants and tech upgrades instead of frontline care, leaving communities stranded.

Real reform means slashing red tape, prosecuting Medicare fraudsters, and letting hospitals compete—not recycling taxpayer cash through the same broken bureaucracy.
